script.opening: "Doctor, I got this letter saying I've got chronic kidney disease and I've been beside myself. My neighbour had kidney disease and ended up on dialysis three times a week, and then… well. Am I heading for that? How long have my kidneys got? I feel fine, so I don't understand how my kidneys can be diseased. I didn't sleep a wink after that letter came."

facts.text: If asked: it arrived on Tuesday, a standard letter saying your recent blood test showed "chronic kidney disease stage 3a" and asking you to book a review. Nobody had mentioned kidneys to you before.
None. You feel well. No swelling, no breathlessness, passing water normally, no blood in the urine, no itching, appetite fine, no weight loss.
High blood pressure for about 10 years and type 2 diabetes for 8 years. "My sugars are okay, the nurse says." Home BP readings "usually around 140 over 85".
Amlodipine and metformin. No allergies. If asked about painkillers: "I take ibuprofen for my knees now and again — a few times a week." You did not know it could matter for the kidneys.
64, retired school cook, widowed, lives alone, close to your daughter and two grandchildren. Never smoked, rarely drinks. Walks to the shops daily.
Mrs Okafor next door had kidney failure, was on dialysis three times a week for two years and died last spring. "She went downhill so fast."

You are frightened of becoming a burden on your daughter and losing your independence. You also feel guilty: "I suppose I brought this on myself with the diabetes — all those years of cakes at work." Say these only if asked what worries you most, or if the doctor is warm and unhurried.

Tearful and anxious at the start. If the doctor jumps straight into numbers, get confused: "I don't understand what that means." If they explain in plain words that this is a mild, stable change and that most people at this stage never need dialysis, you relax and start asking practical questions ("So what can I do?"). If told "it's nothing to worry about" without explanation, stay unconvinced: "Then why did they send me a letter?"

ice.ideas: "Kidney disease means my kidneys are failing and I'll end up on dialysis like Mrs Okafor."
ice.concerns: "How long have my kidneys got?" Underneath: being a burden on your daughter, and guilt that you caused it.
ice.expectations: To be told honestly what is going to happen to you. You would welcome a clear plan of what you can do to protect your kidneys.

cues: "Am I heading for dialysis?" — say in the opening.
"I didn't sleep a wink." — say in the opening; shows the distress.
"I suppose I brought this on myself." — say quietly if diabetes or lifestyle comes up.

checkpoints.text: Explains CKD3a ACCURATELY and reassuringly: a mild reduction in kidney filtering that is common (especially with age, blood pressure and diabetes), here STABLE, and that the large majority of people at this stage NEVER need dialysis — without either minimising or catastrophising

Reframes the "disease" label and the dialysis fear directly: distinguishes her stable CKD3a from the neighbour’s end-stage disease, and explains CKD at this stage is largely a cardiovascular RISK marker to act on, not a countdown to dialysis

Lays out the PROTECTIVE plan: optimise blood pressure and diabetes, ACE inhibitor/ARB where indicated (NICE NG203: with diabetes, offer if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more; NICE NG136 also favours one first-line in hypertension with type 2 diabetes, so her amlodipine-only plan is reviewed), avoid nephrotoxins (NSAIDs), offer a statin (NICE NG238: atorvastatin 20 mg), medication-dose review, and explains the monitoring (periodic eGFR + ACR) as surveillance that catches change early
Addresses GUILT and lifestyle without shaming, and gives realistic, empowering actions (BP, glucose, avoiding ibuprofen, hydration) framed as protecting her kidneys

Knows the genuine NICE NG203 referral criteria (5-year kidney failure risk over 5% on the KFRE; ACR 70 mg/mmol or more unless diabetes is already appropriately treated; ACR 30 or more with haematuria; a sustained eGFR fall of 25% or more with a change of category, or 15 mL/min/1.73 m² or more within 12 months; hypertension uncontrolled on 4 or more drugs; suspected rare or genetic cause) that WOULD warrant nephrology referral — distinguishing her stable picture from those
Responds to the distress and the sleepless fear FIRST, dismantles the neighbour-driven catastrophe with empathy, and replaces dread with an accurate, empowering narrative
Acknowledges the harm of a cold letter without a conversation, and the burden/independence fears, validating them while reassuring

Safety-nets and follows up: the monitoring plan and what change would prompt review, avoiding NSAIDs, when to seek help (e.g. with intercurrent illness/dehydration — sick-day guidance for relevant meds), and a follow-up that leaves her reassured and engaged rather than terrified

worked.txt: "I’m so sorry that letter frightened you and cost you a night’s sleep — let me put the scary word in proportion straightaway. ‘Chronic kidney disease stage 3’ sounds dramatic, but in your case it means your kidneys are filtering a little slower than a younger person’s — which is incredibly common at 64, especially with blood pressure and diabetes — and yours has been STABLE for a year. This is a world away from your neighbour’s situation."

"Let me answer your real question directly: are you heading for dialysis? Almost certainly not. The vast majority of people at your stage never need it — they live a normal lifespan and die WITH this, not OF it. Your neighbour had advanced, end-stage kidney failure; you have a mild, stable reduction. They’re genuinely different things, and I don’t want you carrying her ending as if it were yours."

"Here’s the useful way to think about it: this number is mostly a nudge to look after your heart and circulation, which protect your kidneys too. So we keep your blood pressure and diabetes well controlled, we use a tablet that shields the kidneys if your urine test shows it’s right for you, we offer a cholesterol tablet to protect your heart, we avoid things that strain them — like ibuprofen — and we keep an eye with a blood and urine test now and then. That’s not a countdown; that’s you in the driving seat."

"And if any part of you is blaming yourself — the diabetes, your diet — please don’t. Kidneys naturally slow with age and blood pressure; this isn’t a punishment. What matters now is the things we CAN do, and there’s plenty, and they work."

"I’ll be straight: we do keep watching, because occasionally kidney function drifts, and we’d rather catch that early. So you’ll have periodic tests. If the numbers ever changed in a way that needed a specialist, we’d arrange that — but you are nowhere near that, and stable is exactly what we want."

"One practical thing: avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen — paracetamol’s fine — and if you’re ever really unwell with vomiting or diarrhoea, drink plenty and let us know, as we sometimes pause certain tablets briefly. Otherwise, please sleep tonight: this is mild, stable, and managed. Come and see me to go through it properly and ask anything — you are going to be absolutely fine looking after this."

f.learning: A CKD stage-3a result (eGFR ~52, stable, ACR normal/mildly raised) in a well 64-year-old is a RISK-COMMUNICATION consultation: the word "disease" in a letter, with no conversation, lands as a dialysis-and-death sentence — here amplified by a neighbour’s end-stage disease mapped onto herself. The task is to reframe ACCURATELY without minimising: CKD3a is common (age, BP, diabetes), usually stable, the large majority never need dialysis (they die with it, not of it), and at this stage it is largely a cardiovascular risk marker to act on. Lay out the protective levers (BP and diabetes control, ACE inhibitor/ARB where indicated — NICE NG203: with diabetes, if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more — avoid NSAIDs, atorvastatin 20 mg per NICE NG238, dose review, periodic eGFR+ACR monitoring), address guilt without shaming, and know the genuine NICE NG203 referral criteria (5-year kidney failure risk over 5%, ACR 70 or more, ACR 30 or more with haematuria, a sustained significant eGFR fall, hypertension uncontrolled on 4 or more drugs, suspected rare or genetic cause) that distinguish her stable picture from those needing nephrology. Respond to the distress first, dismantle the neighbour-driven catastrophe, and safety-net (NSAID avoidance, sick-day guidance, monitoring) so she leaves reassured and engaged. eGFR 52 (CKD stage 3a) that is STABLE over a year with normal/mildly-raised ACR is common, usually age- and blood-pressure-related, and the large majority of people at this stage NEVER need dialysis and die WITH it, not OF it. The label "disease" frightens people far more than the mild, manageable reality. If reached: nobody explained the result before the letter; the term landed as a death sentence. The consultation is largely RISK COMMUNICATION — reframing a number into a manageable, mostly-stable condition without either minimising or terrifying.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE TA1075 (2025) · NICE NG238 (2023) · NICE NG136 (2019) · KDIGO (international)
knowledge.summary: A stable eGFR of 52 is CKD G3a. For most people at this stage it is a marker of cardiovascular risk to act on, not a path to dialysis. Classify by eGFR and ACR, protect the kidneys and the heart, and explain it without alarm.

points.t: NICE NG203 uses eGFR category (G3a = 45–59) and ACR category (A1 under 3, A2 3–30, A3 over 30 mg/mmol). CKD needs abnormality for more than 3 months; hers is stable over a year. Risk of progression rises with falling eGFR and, above all, with rising ACR.

NICE NG203: with diabetes, offer an ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more; with hypertension and no diabetes, if ACR is over 30. Check potassium and eGFR before and after starting. Her ACR needs an exact repeat value to decide.

Offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention in CKD (NICE NG238). With type 2 diabetes, dapagliflozin is an option in CKD within NICE TA1075 (2025) criteria, on top of optimised standard care. NG203 blood-pressure target when ACR is under 70: 120–139/under 90 mmHg. In hypertension with type 2 diabetes, NICE NG136 favours an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first choice, so review the current amlodipine-only plan.

Avoid NSAIDs. Review renally cleared drugs: the BNF advises reviewing the metformin dose when eGFR falls below 45 and avoiding it below 30. Give sick-day guidance for metformin (and any ACE inhibitor, ARB or SGLT2 inhibitor): pause during dehydrating illness and restart after 24–48 hours of eating and drinking normally.

NICE NG203 suggests at least yearly eGFR for G3a with ACR under 3 (more often as ACR rises). Refer if: ACR 70 or more (unless diabetes already appropriately treated); ACR 30 or more with haematuria; sustained eGFR fall of 25% or more with a change of category, or 15 mL/min/1.73 m² or more within 12 months; hypertension uncontrolled on 4 or more drugs; suspected rare or genetic cause; 5-year kidney failure risk over 5%. None apply to her now.

Patients hear ‘chronic kidney disease’ as kidney failure. Put the stage in proportion, address specific fears (here a neighbour on dialysis), avoid both false reassurance and alarm, and turn the label into things she can do.

model.text: Hello, is that Mrs Patricia Nwosu? It’s Dr Lee. Could you confirm your date of birth? Thank you. I understand you’ve had a letter that’s upset you. Tell me what’s happened.
model.why: Confirms identity, then opens with her experience

model.text: Doctor, it said I’ve got chronic kidney disease. I’ve been beside myself. My neighbour had kidney disease and ended up on dialysis three times a week, and then… well. Am I heading for that? How long have my kidneys got? I didn’t sleep a wink.

I’m really sorry. That letter should have come with a conversation, and it’s cost you a night’s sleep. Let me say straight away: from what I can see, I’m not expecting you to need dialysis. I’ll explain why, and then we’ll go through what it does mean. Is that alright?
model.why: Acknowledges the harm of the letter and answers the core fear early

model.text: (Exhales.) Yes. Please.

Can I check a few things first so my explanation is right for you? How have you been in yourself: any swelling of your ankles, passing water more at night, blood in your urine, or feeling unusually tired?
model.why: Screens for symptoms and haematuria that would change the picture

model.text: No, nothing. I feel fine. That’s what I don’t understand.
And do you ever take anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen or naproxen, or any remedies from the chemist?
Not really. Paracetamol now and then.
That’s good. You’re on amlodipine and metformin. Are you managing to take those, and do you know how your blood pressure and sugar have been?
model.why: Reviews adherence and control of the main drivers

model.text: I take them every day. The nurse said my sugar was alright. Blood pressure’s okay, I think.
You mentioned your neighbour. What worries you most about what happened to her?
model.why: Explores the specific fear rather than reassuring generically

model.text: Being tied to a machine. Being a burden on my family. Losing my independence. And I keep thinking I did this to myself, with the diabetes.

Thank you for telling me. Those are big fears, and it makes sense you’d think of her. Can I take them one at a time? First, the blame. Kidneys slow down naturally with age and with blood pressure. This isn’t a punishment for anything you’ve done.
model.why: Validates, then addresses guilt without shaming

model.text: (Quiet.) I have been blaming myself.

Here’s what the numbers mean. Your kidney filtering score is 52. That puts you in stage 3a, a mild reduction that’s very common at 64, especially with blood pressure and diabetes. The important thing is it’s been steady for a whole year. Your neighbour had kidney failure, which is a different place altogether.
model.why: Accurate staging, stability and distinction from end-stage disease

model.text: So I won’t end up on dialysis?

Most people at your stage never need dialysis. Many live with this for the rest of their lives without it ever causing trouble. I can’t promise anyone the future, which is why we check it, but the realistic outlook is good. What this result mostly tells us is to look after your heart and circulation, because that protects the kidneys too.
model.why: Honest risk communication, neither minimising nor catastrophising

model.text: That’s not what I read online.
Online pages often describe the worst cases. Your results, and the fact they’re stable, are what count.
model.why: Corrects misinformation briefly and anchors to her own data

model.text: There are three things that protect your kidneys. First, I’d like to repeat the urine protein test so we have an exact number. If there’s even a small amount of protein, with diabetes it’s worth adding a tablet that shields the kidneys, and it would help your blood pressure too. Second, a cholesterol tablet to protect your heart. Third, there’s a diabetes tablet that also protects the kidneys, which we can discuss. How does that sound?
model.why: Protective plan by ACR: ACE inhibitor or ARB, statin, SGLT2 inhibitor option

model.text: That’s a lot of tablets. But if it protects them… I’d rather do something than just worry.
We don’t need to decide everything today. Let’s get the urine test, then go through the options face to face so you can choose what feels right. Would you like me to book that?
model.why: Shared decision, paced to her; offers a face-to-face review

model.text: Yes, I’d like that.

Two practical things. Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen; paracetamol is fine. And if you’re ever unwell with vomiting, diarrhoea or a fever and can’t keep fluids down, stop the metformin and restart it once you’ve been eating and drinking normally for a day or two. Ring us if you’re unwell for more than a day or so.
We’ll check your kidney numbers at least once a year. If they ever changed in a way that needed a specialist, we’d spot it early and arrange it. At the moment you’re nowhere near that.
model.why: Explains monitoring as early detection and states referral triggers exist

model.text: That’s such a relief.
If someone in your family asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
model.why: Teach-back checks the reframe has landed

model.text: That it’s mild and steady, it’s not like my neighbour, and we’re doing things to protect my kidneys and heart. And no ibuprofen.
That’s exactly right. I’ll book the urine test and an appointment with me afterwards. Please try to sleep tonight.
model.why: Warm close with a booked follow-up

social.t: Her fear is of becoming a burden and losing independence. Framing the plan as protecting her independence is more persuasive than numbers.
She has read worst-case material online. Point her to reliable UK patient information and anchor the discussion to her own stable results.

legal.t: Discuss material risks and reasonable alternatives before starting an ACE inhibitor, statin or SGLT2 inhibitor, and respect her choice (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board, 2015).

professional.t: A diagnostic label sent by letter without discussion caused avoidable distress. Acknowledge it honestly and consider it for practice learning (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: communication and openness).
Pace decisions to the patient and offer a face-to-face review for a new long-term diagnosis (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Kidney Care UK and Diabetes UK patient information; community pharmacy advice on avoiding NSAIDs; annual flu vaccine as she has diabetes (UKHSA Green Book).

redFlags: Visible or non-visible haematuria with the CKD — changes the referral threshold
Rapid fall in eGFR, rising ACR, or new oedema — needs review and possible referral
Regular NSAID use or dehydrating illness — risk of acute kidney injury
psychosocial: Sleepless and frightened after a letter with no conversation
Neighbour’s dialysis and death mapped onto herself
Fear of being a burden and losing independence; guilt about diabetes
ice: Idea: her kidneys are failing and dialysis is coming
Concern: becoming a burden, losing independence, having caused it herself
Expectation: to be told how long her kidneys have left

playbook.diagnosis: Give the accurate picture: “You have stage 3a chronic kidney disease. It’s mild, it’s been steady for a year, and for most people at this stage it never leads to dialysis. It’s a signal to protect your heart and kidneys.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of your kidneys as a filter that’s running a little slower than it did when you were 30, like most people’s at 64. It’s been steady all year. Your neighbour’s filter had stopped working; yours is doing its job, and we’ll help it keep doing it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened of ending up like your neighbour and of being a burden. That’s not where you are, and the plan we’re making is about keeping you well and independent.”
management.psychosocial: Lift the guilt, correct the online worst-case picture, and pace the medicines discussion so she chooses rather than feels prescribed at.
sharedPlan: Repeat ACR; ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR 3 mg/mmol or more with diabetes (NICE NG203)
Atorvastatin 20 mg (NICE NG238); discuss dapagliflozin (NICE TA1075, 2025); BP and HbA1c optimised
Avoid NSAIDs; metformin dose review if eGFR falls below 45 (BNF)
safetyNet: Sick-day guidance for metformin during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
At least yearly eGFR and ACR; referral if NG203 criteria are met; booked face-to-face review

pitfalls.intro: This is a risk-communication station. It is failed by minimising (“stage 3 is nothing”), by leaving the dialysis fear standing, or by a plan that ignores ACR. The marks sit in accurate reassurance plus a real protective plan.

items.fail: Launching into eGFR and stages before acknowledging her distress and the letter.
items.why: She cannot take in numbers while frightened. “Did not respond to the patient’s emotional state” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Acknowledge the sleepless night and the letter, and answer the dialysis question briefly first.

items.fail: Saying “don’t worry” without asking about the neighbour.
items.why: The neighbour’s story is the source of the fear. Generic reassurance doesn’t reach it.
items.fix: “What worries you most about what happened to her?” Then contrast kidney failure with her stable G3a.

items.why: With diabetes, NICE NG203 recommends an ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more; statin and SGLT2 inhibitor are also indicated options. A passive plan misses real protection.
items.fix: Repeat ACR and set out the three protective options for her to choose.

items.fail: Promising she will never need dialysis.
items.why: False certainty is inaccurate and undermines monitoring.
items.fix: “Most people at your stage never need it. We keep checking so any change is caught early.”

items.why: These are the practical safety measures examiners expect in any CKD consultation.
items.fix: Paracetamol, not ibuprofen; pause metformin during dehydrating illness and restart after 24–48 hours of normal eating and drinking.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Your kidney filtering score” and “a urine test for protein”; then teach-back.

Symptoms, haematuria, NSAIDs, adherence, BP and glucose control.
What worries her most about the neighbour’s story. Burden, independence, blame. Lift the guilt.

wordPics.fail: Reads out the stage and “it’s nothing to worry about”; never asks about the neighbour; or leaves her thinking dialysis is likely; no ACR plan; no NSAID or sick-day advice; ends without follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Explains CKD 3a accurately as mild and stable; distinguishes it from kidney failure; outlines BP, diabetes and NSAID advice; plans monitoring and a review.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: explores and dismantles the neighbour fear and the guilt; uses ACR to decide on an ACE inhibitor or ARB; offers statin and SGLT2 inhibitor as choices at her pace; gives sick-day guidance; checks understanding with teach-back.

avoid.why: Minimising loses her trust and removes the reason to engage with the protective plan.

avoid.dont: “Your kidneys are only working at about half.”
avoid.instead: “Your kidneys are filtering a little slower than a younger person’s, which is common at 64.”
avoid.why: ‘Half’ sounds like failure to a frightened patient; describe the reality, not a fraction.

avoid.why: A list of drug names on the phone to a distressed patient is not shared decision-making.

SCA_MODELS.why: Corrects misinformation briefly and anchors to her own data

SCA_MODELS.text: There are three things that protect your kidneys. First, I’d like to repeat the urine protein test so we have an exact number. If there’s even a small amount of protein, with diabetes it’s worth adding a tablet that shields the kidneys, and it would help your blood pressure too. Second, a cholesterol tablet to protect your heart. Third, there’s a diabetes tablet that also protects the kidneys, which we can discuss. How does that sound?
SCA_MODELS.why: Protective plan by ACR: ACE inhibitor or ARB, statin, SGLT2 inhibitor option

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s a lot of tablets. But if it protects them… I’d rather do something than just worry.
We don’t need to decide everything today. Let’s get the urine test, then go through the options face to face so you can choose what feels right. Would you like me to book that?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shared decision, paced to her; offers a face-to-face review

SCA_MODELS.text: Yes, I’d like that.

Two practical things. Avoid anti-inflammatory painkillers like ibuprofen; paracetamol is fine. And if you’re ever unwell with vomiting, diarrhoea or a fever and can’t keep fluids down, stop the metformin and restart it once you’ve been eating and drinking normally for a day or two. Ring us if you’re unwell for more than a day or so.
We’ll check your kidney numbers at least once a year. If they ever changed in a way that needed a specialist, we’d spot it early and arrange it. At the moment you’re nowhere near that.
SCA_MODELS.why: Explains monitoring as early detection and states referral triggers exist

SCA_MODELS.text: That’s such a relief.
If someone in your family asks tonight what the doctor said, what will you tell them?
SCA_MODELS.why: Teach-back checks the reframe has landed

SCA_MODELS.text: That it’s mild and steady, it’s not like my neighbour, and we’re doing things to protect my kidneys and heart. And no ibuprofen.
That’s exactly right. I’ll book the urine test and an appointment with me afterwards. Please try to sleep tonight.
SCA_MODELS.why: Warm close with a booked follow-up

SCA_STEM.name: Patricia Nwosu
pmh: Chronic kidney disease stage 3a (newly coded at routine review)
SCA_STEM.recent: Routine long-term condition review: eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m², stable over the past year. Urine ACR normal to mildly raised. A results letter was sent mentioning ‘chronic kidney disease’. No consultation since.
SCA_STEM.reason: Telephoned the surgery upset after receiving the letter. Asking to speak to a doctor today.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG203 (2021) · NICE TA1075 (2025) · NICE NG238 (2023) · NICE NG136 (2019) · KDIGO (international)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A stable eGFR of 52 is CKD G3a. For most people at this stage it is a marker of cardiovascular risk to act on, not a path to dialysis. Classify by eGFR and ACR, protect the kidneys and the heart, and explain it without alarm.

points.t: NICE NG203 uses eGFR category (G3a = 45–59) and ACR category (A1 under 3, A2 3–30, A3 over 30 mg/mmol). CKD needs abnormality for more than 3 months; hers is stable over a year. Risk of progression rises with falling eGFR and, above all, with rising ACR.

NICE NG203: with diabetes, offer an ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more; with hypertension and no diabetes, if ACR is over 30. Check potassium and eGFR before and after starting. Her ACR needs an exact repeat value to decide.

Offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention in CKD (NICE NG238). With type 2 diabetes, dapagliflozin is an option in CKD within NICE TA1075 (2025) criteria, on top of optimised standard care. NG203 blood-pressure target when ACR is under 70: 120–139/under 90 mmHg. In hypertension with type 2 diabetes, NICE NG136 favours an ACE inhibitor or ARB as first choice, so review the current amlodipine-only plan.

Avoid NSAIDs. Review renally cleared drugs: the BNF advises reviewing the metformin dose when eGFR falls below 45 and avoiding it below 30. Give sick-day guidance for metformin (and any ACE inhibitor, ARB or SGLT2 inhibitor): pause during dehydrating illness and restart after 24–48 hours of eating and drinking normally.

NICE NG203 suggests at least yearly eGFR for G3a with ACR under 3 (more often as ACR rises). Refer if: ACR 70 or more (unless diabetes already appropriately treated); ACR 30 or more with haematuria; sustained eGFR fall of 25% or more with a change of category, or 15 mL/min/1.73 m² or more within 12 months; hypertension uncontrolled on 4 or more drugs; suspected rare or genetic cause; 5-year kidney failure risk over 5%. None apply to her now.

Patients hear ‘chronic kidney disease’ as kidney failure. Put the stage in proportion, address specific fears (here a neighbour on dialysis), avoid both false reassurance and alarm, and turn the label into things she can do.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Confirmed identity; open question about the letter; let her voice the dialysis fear before explaining.
Sleep lost, fear of being a burden, loss of independence, the neighbour’s illness, online reading.
Picked up ‘and then… well’ about the neighbour and ‘I did this to myself’, and explored both.
Idea (kidney failure, dialysis); concern (burden, independence, guilt); expectation (to know how long her kidneys have).
Repeat ACR for an exact value; BP and HbA1c review; lipids and cardiovascular risk; yearly eGFR monitoring.
Stable CKD G3a from age, hypertension and diabetes; asked about haematuria, NSAIDs and symptoms.
Checked for haematuria, oedema and rapid decline; knew the NG203 referral criteria and that none apply.
CKD stage 3a, stable, low progression risk; explained as a cardiovascular risk marker.
ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR 3 or more with diabetes; statin; SGLT2 inhibitor discussed; choices paced to her.
BP and diabetes control, metformin dose review threshold, NSAID avoidance.
Sick-day guidance, monitoring plan, booked review, teach-back.

social.t: Her fear is of becoming a burden and losing independence. Framing the plan as protecting her independence is more persuasive than numbers.
She has read worst-case material online. Point her to reliable UK patient information and anchor the discussion to her own stable results.

legal.t: Discuss material risks and reasonable alternatives before starting an ACE inhibitor, statin or SGLT2 inhibitor, and respect her choice (Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board, 2015).

professional.t: A diagnostic label sent by letter without discussion caused avoidable distress. Acknowledge it honestly and consider it for practice learning (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024: communication and openness).
Pace decisions to the patient and offer a face-to-face review for a new long-term diagnosis (GMC Decision making and consent, 2020).

community.t: Kidney Care UK and Diabetes UK patient information; community pharmacy advice on avoiding NSAIDs; annual flu vaccine as she has diabetes (UKHSA Green Book).

redFlags: Visible or non-visible haematuria with the CKD — changes the referral threshold
Rapid fall in eGFR, rising ACR, or new oedema — needs review and possible referral
Regular NSAID use or dehydrating illness — risk of acute kidney injury
psychosocial: Sleepless and frightened after a letter with no conversation
Neighbour’s dialysis and death mapped onto herself
Fear of being a burden and losing independence; guilt about diabetes
ice: Idea: her kidneys are failing and dialysis is coming
Concern: becoming a burden, losing independence, having caused it herself
Expectation: to be told how long her kidneys have left

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Give the accurate picture: “You have stage 3a chronic kidney disease. It’s mild, it’s been steady for a year, and for most people at this stage it never leads to dialysis. It’s a signal to protect your heart and kidneys.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of your kidneys as a filter that’s running a little slower than it did when you were 30, like most people’s at 64. It’s been steady all year. Your neighbour’s filter had stopped working; yours is doing its job, and we’ll help it keep doing it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were frightened of ending up like your neighbour and of being a burden. That’s not where you are, and the plan we’re making is about keeping you well and independent.”
management.psychosocial: Lift the guilt, correct the online worst-case picture, and pace the medicines discussion so she chooses rather than feels prescribed at.
sharedPlan: Repeat ACR; ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR 3 mg/mmol or more with diabetes (NICE NG203)
Atorvastatin 20 mg (NICE NG238); discuss dapagliflozin (NICE TA1075, 2025); BP and HbA1c optimised
Avoid NSAIDs; metformin dose review if eGFR falls below 45 (BNF)
safetyNet: Sick-day guidance for metformin during vomiting, diarrhoea or fever
At least yearly eGFR and ACR; referral if NG203 criteria are met; booked face-to-face review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This is a risk-communication station. It is failed by minimising (“stage 3 is nothing”), by leaving the dialysis fear standing, or by a plan that ignores ACR. The marks sit in accurate reassurance plus a real protective plan.

items.fail: Launching into eGFR and stages before acknowledging her distress and the letter.
items.why: She cannot take in numbers while frightened. “Did not respond to the patient’s emotional state” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Acknowledge the sleepless night and the letter, and answer the dialysis question briefly first.

items.fail: Saying “don’t worry” without asking about the neighbour.
items.why: The neighbour’s story is the source of the fear. Generic reassurance doesn’t reach it.
items.fix: “What worries you most about what happened to her?” Then contrast kidney failure with her stable G3a.

items.why: With diabetes, NICE NG203 recommends an ACE inhibitor or ARB if ACR is 3 mg/mmol or more; statin and SGLT2 inhibitor are also indicated options. A passive plan misses real protection.
items.fix: Repeat ACR and set out the three protective options for her to choose.

items.fail: Promising she will never need dialysis.
items.why: False certainty is inaccurate and undermines monitoring.
items.fix: “Most people at your stage never need it. We keep checking so any change is caught early.”

items.why: These are the practical safety measures examiners expect in any CKD consultation.
items.fix: Paracetamol, not ibuprofen; pause metformin during dehydrating illness and restart after 24–48 hours of normal eating and drinking.

items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: “Your kidney filtering score” and “a urine test for protein”; then teach-back.
